```{r}
#| label: setup

set.seed(54321)

# Output -----------------------------------------------------------------------
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center")

# Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------------
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tinytable)

library(rosdata)

# Functions --------------------------------------------------------------------
source(here::here("R/simulate_correlation.R"))
source(here::here("R/make_hibbs_plot.R"))

# Theme ------------------------------------------------------------------------
theme_st303 <- function() {
  theme_bw() +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = rel(1.1), face = "bold"),
      axis.title = element_text(size = rel(0.8), face = "bold"),
      legend.title.position = "top",
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = rel(0.8), face = "bold"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}

# Datasets ---------------------------------------------------------------------
anscombe_data <- datasets::anscombe |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = c(".value", "dataset"),
    names_pattern = "([xy])([1-4])"
  )

# Father and son heights
father_son <- read.table(here::here("data/father_son.txt"), header = TRUE)
```

## Todays lecture {style="font-size:90%;"}

[**We want to understand how two quantitative variables are related**]{.center}

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

- Interpret the direction and strength of a correlation
- Calculate and interpret the sample correlation coefficient
- Explain why scatterplots are essential when interpreting correlation
- Connect correlation to simple linear regression and $R^2$
- Explain regression towards the mean
- Distinguish correlation from regression and understand why the direction
  of regression matters

## Let's start with a scatter plot

```{r}
#| label: example-scatter-plot

# Make up some data
example_data <- tibble(x = rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)) |>
  mutate(y = 1.2 * x + rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 0.9))

# Plot that data
example_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_st303()
```


::: {.callout-note}
## Question: What do you notice about the relationship between (X) and (Y)?
:::

## Describing a relationship {style="font-size: 80%;"}

When examining a scatterplot, we typically consider three things


::: {.fragment .fade-down}

**Direction**

- **Positive**: larger values of (X) tend to accompany larger values of (Y)
- **Negative**: larger values of (X) tend to accompany smaller values of (Y)

:::


::: {.fragment .fade-right}

**Strength**

- **Strong**: observations follow a relatively clear pattern
- **Weak**: observations are more dispersed around the overall pattern

:::


::: {.fragment .fade-up}

**Form**

- **Linear**: the relationship follows an approximately straight-line pattern.
- **Nonlinear**: the relationship follows a curve or another pattern.

:::

---

<br>

```{r}
#| label: correlation-examples
#|
# Different kinds of correlations
corr_examples <- purrr::map_dfr(
  c(-0.9, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 0.9),
  simulate_correlation
)

# Plot them all out
corr_examples |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~target) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    tag = "The correlation defines the <br>strength of the association",
  ) +
  theme_st303() +
  theme(
    plot.tag = ggtext::element_textbox_simple(
      hjust = 0,
      halign = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 5, t = 5),
      maxwidth = 0.5,
      lineheight = 1.15,
      face = "bold",
      size = rel(1.5)
    ),
    plot.tag.position = c(0.70, 0.25),
  )
```

## The correlation coefficient {style="font-size:70%;"}

The sample correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of the
linear association between two quantitative variables

$$
r = \frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \times S_{yy}}}
$$

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}

- **Bounded**: $-1 \leq r \leq 1$
- **Direction**:
  - $r > 0$ indicates positive linear association
  - $r < 0$ indicates negative linear association
- **Strength**: Values closer to $-1$ or $1$ indicate stronger linear association.
- **Symmetry**: $\operatorname{cor}(X,Y)=\operatorname{cor}(Y,X)$
- **Unit-free**: Correlation is unaffected by changing the measurement units


::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
## A correlation of zero means there is no linear association

It does not rule out a nonlinear relationship
:::
::::

---

<br>

```{r}
#| label: non-linear-correlation

# Create a non-linear data
nonlinear_data <- tibble(x = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 150)) |>
  mutate(y = x^2 + rnorm(n(), sd = 0.8))

# Plot it out
nonlinear_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_st303()
```

::: {.notes}
- The relationship is clearly nonlinear, even though the Pearson correlation
  can be close to zero.
- A near-zero correlation does not necessarily mean that the variables
  are unrelated.
- **Takeaway**: always inspect the scatterplot before interpreting a
  correlation coefficient.
:::

## Summary statistics

<br>

```{r}
#| label: anscombe-table
anscombe_data |>
  group_by(dataset) |>
  summarise(
    mean_x = mean(x),
    sd_x = sd(x),
    mean_y = mean(y),
    sd_y = sd(y),
    r = cor(x, y)
  ) |>
  mutate(dataset = paste("Dataset", 1:4)) |>
  tt(digits = 3, width = 0.75, theme = "empty") |>
  setNames(c("Dataset", "Mean", "SD", "Mean", "SD", "r")) |>
  group_tt(j = list("X variable" = 2:3, "Y variable" = 4:5)) |>
  style_tt(i = c(-1, 0), bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(j = 2:6, align = "c")
```

## Data visualisation

```{r}
#| label: anscombe-plot-1a
anscombe_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(size = rel(1.2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~dataset,
    labeller = labeller(
      dataset = function(x) paste("Dataset", x)
    )
  ) +
  theme_st303()
```

## Summary statistics

```{r}
#| label: datasaurus-table
datasauRus::datasaurus_dozen |>
  group_by(dataset) |>
  summarise(
    mean_x = mean(x),
    sd_x = sd(x),
    mean_y = mean(y),

  ) |>

```

## Data visualisation

```{r}
#| label: datasaurus_dozen-plot
#| fig-height: 5.5
datasauRus::datasaurus_dozen |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, colour = dataset)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  MetBrewer::scale_colour_met_d(name = "Signac") +
  facet_wrap(
    ~dataset,
    labeller = labeller(dataset = function(x) {
      x |> stringr::str_replace_all("_", " ") |> stringr::str_to_title()
    }
  )) +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  theme_st303()
```

:::

## Correlation and $R^2$ {style="font-size:90%;"}

Recall that the formula for $R^2$ is

$$
R^2 = \frac{SS_R}{SS_T} \qquad \text{OR} \qquad R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS_E}{SS_T}
$$

It describes the proportion of the observed variation in $Y$ accounted for by
the fitted linear model


::: {.fragment .fade-up}

$$
R^2 = r^2
$$
For example, if we got $r = 0.8$, then we can say that $R^2 = 0.64$

The fitted linear model accounts for 64% of the variation in the response
around its mean

:::

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## Two datasets have correlations of 0.8 and −0.8

Do they have the same $R^2$?
:::
::::

## Correlation and $R^2$

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
## Word of caution

Two $R^2$ values may be similar even when the relationships have different
structures

A high $R^2$ does not guarantee that a linear model is appropriate

**Always consider the scatterplot and relevant model assumptions**
:::

```{r}
#| label: anscombe-plot-1b
anscombe_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~dataset,
    labeller = labeller(
      dataset = function(x) paste("Dataset", x)
    )
  ) +
  theme_st303()
```

## Let's do an application

### The Hibbs dataset

<br>

```{r}
#| label: hibbs-plot
make_hibbs_plot(hibbs = hibbs)
```

## Let's do an application

### The Hibbs dataset

```{r}
#| label: modelling-hibbs
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

# Calculate a correlation coefficient between economic growth and voting percentage
cor(hibbs$growth, hibbs$vote)

# Turn this into an R squared statistic
cor(hibbs$growth, hibbs$vote)^2

# Fit a simple linear model and verify the statistic
voting_model <- lm(vote ~ growth, data = hibbs)

summary(voting_model)
```

## Regression towards the mean

<br>

```{r}
#| label: father-son-plot-1a
father_son |>
  as_tibble() |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = father, y = son)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Height of father", y = "Height of son") +
  theme_st303()
```

## Regression towards the mean

<br>

```{r}
#| label: father-son-plot-1b
father_son |>
  as_tibble() |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = father, y = son)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Height of father", y = "Height of son") +
  theme_st303()
```

## Regression towards the mean

<br>

```{r}
#| label: father-son-plot-1c
father_son |>
  as_tibble() |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = father, y = son)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    colour = "#009E73"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Height of father", y = "Height of son") +
  theme_st303()
```

## Regression towards the mean

### What is it

- Suppose a father is substantially taller than the population average
- His son is expected to be taller than average too, because heights are
  positively associated
- However, the predicted son's height is typically closer to the population
  mean than the father's height is, when both are measured on the same scale
  and the fitted slope is between zero and one

[**This is regression towards the mean**]{.center}

This helps explain why extreme observations on one variable tend to be
associated with less extreme expected values of the other variable
